newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai protesters to remain despite meeting PM.
newsitem.headline: Thai protesters to remain despite meeting PM.

text.p: Representatives of thousands of impoverished Thais camped outside Government House for three days to press for social justice met the prime minister on Monday, but refused to disperse until solutions were reached.
"We will live here until our demands are met, I don't care whether it takes weeks or months," said Kamsaen Sertlaho, a protest leader.
Government officials said it could take up to a week just to narrow differences over some of the eight key issues raised by the 10,000 protesters, who come from impoverished northeastern provinces.
The protesters, organised by the so-called Assembly of the Poor movement, streamed into Bangkok last Friday on buses, trains and trucks carrying sacks of food, cooking and camping equipment.

They set up shelters of plastic sheets along two roads flanking Government House, forcing authorities to offer them mobile toilets and medical help. Government House is the office of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh.
The protesters, who come from the area where Chavalit was elected, cook meals on the road and sleep there under the watchful eyes of 600 policemen.

"Ninety percent of their problems are related to a lack of land for farming and I hope most of the problems would be settled during the two-year tenure of my government," said Chavalit at a meeting with 150 representatives of the protesters at Government House.

"But I would like to remind the Assembly that you had better limit your role to minding about the plight of the poor only," he said referring to 120 other political and trade issues raised by the protesters.

The protesters want the government to resolve land disputes with the authorities, raise the purchase price of the tapioca they farm and free them of debts they owe to the state-owned Agriculture and Cooperatives Bank.

But they also want the government to renegotiate some clauses it has agreed with the World Trade Organisation to liberalise trade, saying such agreements harm Thai farmers. They also want speedy political reform.
The protesters' representatives disagreed with Chavalit.

"One cannot limit the role of the poor people because poverty not only results from a lack of land but also results from the government's projects and policies," said one representative, Vithaya Damrongsuk.
Chavalit assigned Chingchai Mongkoltham, Minister in the Prime Minister's Office, to chair a panel to set an agenda and hold discussions with Assembly representatives.
"It would take at least one week of discussion to reach a conclusion on the eight points that also cover 120 sub-issues," Chingchai told Reuters.
As their representatives met at Government House, protesters vowed to remain until their demands were met.

A doctor at the protest site said about 100 protesters had received medical treatment for colds and stress. He warned that if the protesters continued to camp on the streets, other diseases and diarrhoea epidemics could break out.
Although the presence of the protesters in the heart of Bangkok has irritated some politicians, Thailand's army commander in chief said they had a right to protest.
"As long as they stage a peaceful rally and do not create trouble, they have the right to do so," General Chettha Tanajaro, told reporters.
